**Taiwan–United States relations** is unofficial and informal. Both sides maintain representative offices functioning as *de facto* embassies. [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan") is represented by the [Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taipei_Economic_and_Cultural_Representative_Office_in_the_United_States "Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office in the United States"),[[1]](#cite_note-1) while the U.S. government is represented by the [American Institute in Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_in_Taiwan "American Institute in Taiwan").[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Taiwan is the United States' ninth largest trading partner.[[3]](#cite_note-3) The U.S. has viewed Taiwan as [geostrategically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geostrategy "Geostrategy") important given its key location in the [first island chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_island_chain "First island chain").[[4]](#cite_note-:02-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5) The [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") follows its [Taiwan Relations Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan_Relations_Act "Taiwan Relations Act") (TRA), which allows it to have relations with the [Taiwanese people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwanese_people "Taiwanese people") and their government, whose name is not specified in that law.[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8)

As stipulated by the TRA, the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") remains the main provider of arms to Taiwan.[[9]](#cite_note-9) The relations have been further grounded in the [Six Assurances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six_Assurances "Six Assurances"), which was a response to the [third communiqué](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Communiqu%C3%A9s#3rd "Three Communiqués") issued when the United States [established diplomatic relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93United_States_relations "China–United States relations") with the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") (PRC) in 1979.

Over the past four decades, the U.S. government's [policy of deliberate ambiguity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Policy_of_deliberate_ambiguity "Policy of deliberate ambiguity") toward Taiwan has been viewed as critical to stabilizing [cross-strait relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-strait_relations "Cross-strait relations") by seeking to deter the PRC from using force toward the region and dissuade [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Taiwan "Geography of Taiwan") from seeking independence.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11) However, in recent years as Beijing escalated its moves and further clarified its intentions, the effectiveness of strategic ambiguity became a topic of debate in academic and policy communities.[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18)

The [Taiwan Travel Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan_Travel_Act "Taiwan Travel Act"), passed by the U.S. Congress on March 16, 2018, allows high-level U.S. officials to visit Taiwan and vice versa.[[19]](#cite_note-19) Both sides have since signed a consular agreement formalizing their existent consular relations on September 13, 2019.[[20]](#cite_note-20) The US government removed self-imposed restrictions on executive branch contacts with Taiwan on January 9, 2021.[[21]](#cite_note-21)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/American_Consulate_Taihoku_Formosa.jpg/250px-American_Consulate_Taihoku_Formosa.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:American_Consulate_Taihoku_Formosa.jpg)

American Consulate in Taihoku, Formosa

Two American diplomats in the 1850s suggested to Washington that the U.S. should obtain the [island of Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_of_Taiwan "Island of Taiwan") from China, but the idea was rejected.[[22]](#cite_note-Gordon2009-22)[[23]](#cite_note-23) Aboriginals in Taiwan often attacked and massacred shipwrecked western sailors, and American diplomats tried to help them. In 1867, during the [*Rover* incident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rover_incident "Rover incident"), a group of [Taiwanese Indigenous people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwanese_indigenous_peoples "Taiwanese indigenous peoples") killed the crew of a wrecked American ship. A subsequent U.S. military expedition attempted retaliation but was defeated in a skirmish, resulting in the death of another American.[[24]](#cite_note-24)[[25]](#cite_note-25)

During the period of [Japanese rule over Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan_under_Japanese_rule "Taiwan under Japanese rule") (then Formosa), the United States operated a consulate in Taihoku (now Taipei), beginning in 1913. The consulate was closed in 1941 due to [United States declaration of war on Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_declaration_of_war_on_Japan "United States declaration of war on Japan"). In 1997, the building, housing the [Taipei Film House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taipei_Film_House "Taipei Film House") was listed as historic monument by the Taiwanese government.[[26]](#cite_note-26)

During the [Pacific War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_War "Pacific War"), the United States and the Republic of China (then based in mainland China) were [allied](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Policemen "Four Policemen") against Japan that was occupying the island of Taiwan (Formosa). As early as 1943, the [United States Army Air Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Air_Forces "United States Army Air Forces") launched several air raids against military and industrial targets in Japanese Taiwan. After American ground forces captured Subic Bay in the Philippines, the Allied air forces began larger and more systematic air raids against targets on the island of Taiwan. On 31 May 1945, units of the Fifth Air Force consisting of 117 Consolidated B-24 Liberator heavy bombers were sent to [conduct the largest air raid ever on Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raid_on_Taipei "Raid on Taipei"). The non-stop bombing began around 10 in the morning and lasted for three hours. The Americans met virtually no resistance from the Japanese, mainly due to the attrition the Japanese air forces had suffered in the [Formosa Air Battle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formosa_Air_Battle "Formosa Air Battle"), which completely exhausted Japan's fighter units in Taiwan. The Allied forces dropped approximately 3,800 bombs on military units and governmental facilities in Taihoku (Taipei), including the Office of the Governor-General of Taiwan (today the Presidential Office Building), and killing more than 3000 civilians.[[27]](#cite_note-27)

In October 1945, a month after [Japan's surrender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrender_of_Japan "Surrender of Japan"), representatives of Chinese leader [Chiang Kai-shek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiang_Kai-shek "Chiang Kai-shek"), on behalf of the [Allies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II"), were sent to Formosa to accept the surrender of [Japanese troops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armed_Forces_of_the_Empire_of_Japan "Armed Forces of the Empire of Japan"). However, during the period of the 1940s, there was no recognition by the [United States Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States "Federal government of the United States") that Taiwan had ever been incorporated into Chinese national territory.[[28]](#cite_note-28) Chiang continued to remain suspicious of America's motives.[[29]](#cite_note-29)

Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea_disputes:
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/South_China_Sea_vector.svg/250px-South_China_Sea_vector.svg.png)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:South_China_Sea_vector.svg)

Map of the [nine-dash line](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine-dash_line "Nine-dash line") and EEZs

[Brunei](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunei "Brunei"), [Indonesia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia"), [Malaysia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia"), the [Philippines](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines"), the [People's Republic of China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") (PRC), [Taiwan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan") (Republic of China/ROC), and [Vietnam](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam "Vietnam") have conflicting island and maritime claims in the [South China Sea](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea "South China Sea"). The disputes involve the islands, reefs, banks, and other features of the region, including the [Spratly Islands](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spratly_Islands "Spratly Islands"), [Paracel Islands](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paracel_Islands "Paracel Islands"), [Scarborough Shoal](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarborough_Shoal "Scarborough Shoal"), and some boundaries in the [Gulf of Tonkin](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Tonkin "Gulf of Tonkin"). The waters near the Indonesian [Natuna Islands](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natuna_Islands "Natuna Islands"), which some regard as geographically part of the South China Sea, are disputed as well.

An estimated US$3.36 trillion worth of [global trade](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_trade "International trade") passes through the South China Sea annually,[[1]](#cite_note-China_Power-2017-1) which accounts for a third of the global maritime trade.[[2]](#cite_note-2) 80 percent of China's energy imports and 40 percent of China's total trade passes through the South China Sea.[[1]](#cite_note-China_Power-2017-1) Claimant states are interested in retaining or acquiring the rights to fishing stocks, the exploration and potential exploitation of [crude oil](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crude_oil "Crude oil") and [natural gas](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas "Natural gas") in the seabed of various parts of the South China Sea, and the strategic control of important [shipping lanes](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shipping_lanes "Shipping lanes"). [Maritime security](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_security "Maritime security") is also an issue, as the ongoing disputes present challenges for shipping.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

According to researchers, claims to any of the features were not seriously made until the 19th or the early 20th century.[[4]](#cite_note-:1-4)[[5]](#cite_note-:2a-5) The Paracel Islands, currently occupied by China, are contested by Taiwan and Vietnam. The Spratly Islands are claimed by all three, where Vietnam occupies the greatest number of features and Taiwan occupies the largest, [Taiping Island](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiping_Island "Taiping Island"). Brunei, Malaysia, and the Philippines also claim some of the features in the island chain.[[6]](#cite_note-:0-6) By the 1970s, the Philippines, Taiwan, and Vietnam had militarily occupied one or more of the Spratly Islands.[[7]](#cite_note-7) By 2015, the PRC had established 8 outposts, Malaysia 5, the Philippines 8, Taiwan 1, and Vietnam 48.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

For decades, the Philippines and Vietnam were the most active in building [artificial islands](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_island "Artificial island") in the area,[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) but from 2014 to 2016 China's construction activity outpaced them.[[11]](#cite_note-Asia_Maritime_Transparency_Initiative-11) By 2023, China had reclaimed around five square miles with its artificial islands, at least one of which housed military equipment.[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[6]](#cite_note-:0-6)

China's actions in the South China Sea have been criticized as part of its "[salami slicing](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_salami_slicing_strategy "Chinese salami slicing strategy")"/"[cabbage wrapping](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabbage_tactics "Cabbage tactics")" strategies.[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14) Since 2015, the United States and other states such as [France](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") and the [United Kingdom](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") have conducted [freedom of navigation operations](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_navigation "Freedom of navigation") (FONOP) in the region.[[15]](#cite_note-15) A 2016 [arbitration tribunal](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea_Arbitration "South China Sea Arbitration"), without determining the sovereignty of any of the islands, concluded that China lacks historical titles to the maritime areas within the [nine-dash line](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine-dash_line "Nine-dash line"). The ruling was rejected by both the PRC and ROC.

Events from the year **2023 in Taiwan**, [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China "Republic of China"). This year is numbered Minguo 112 according to the official [Republic of China calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_calendar "Republic of China calendar").

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

The **Taiwan Strait Crises** refers to conflicts involving the [Republic of China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China "Republic of China") and the [People's Republic of China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China"), following the end of the [Chinese Civil War](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Civil_War "Chinese Civil War").

* The [First Taiwan Strait Crisis](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Taiwan_Strait_Crisis "First Taiwan Strait Crisis") (1954–1955), caused by the [People's Liberation Army](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army "People's Liberation Army") (PLA) [shelling](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrage_(artillery) "Barrage (artillery)") of [Kinmen](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinmen "Kinmen") and later also the [Matsu](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matsu_Islands "Matsu Islands") and [Dachen Islands](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dachen_Islands "Dachen Islands")
* The [Second Taiwan Strait Crisis](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Taiwan_Strait_Crisis "Second Taiwan Strait Crisis") (1958), caused by another large-scale PLA shelling of Kinmen and Matsu
* The [Third Taiwan Strait Crisis](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Taiwan_Strait_Crisis "Third Taiwan Strait Crisis") (1995–1996), in the lead-up to [Lee Teng-hui](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Teng-hui "Lee Teng-hui")'s re-election in the [1996 Taiwanese presidential election](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Taiwanese_presidential_election "1996 Taiwanese presidential election")
* The [Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Taiwan_Strait_Crisis "Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis") (2022–present), a series of large-scale encroaching Chinese military drills around Taiwan, the first of which was triggered by the former [speaker of the United States House of Representatives](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives "Speaker of the United States House of Representatives") [Nancy Pelosi](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi "Nancy Pelosi")'s [visit to Taiwan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_visit_by_Nancy_Pelosi_to_Taiwan "2022 visit by Nancy Pelosi to Taiwan")

The **Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis** ([traditional Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_characters "Traditional Chinese characters"): 第四次臺海危機; [simplified Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters "Simplified Chinese characters"): 第四次台海危机)[[1]](#cite_note-4th_Taiwan_Strait_Crisis-1) is an ongoing conflict between the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") (PRC) and [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan"), officially the Republic of China (ROC), with the PRC conducting several large-scale [military exercises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_exercise "Military exercise") that encircled Taiwan. China initiated military maneuvers around Taiwan on 2 August 2022, before launching their first major military drill on 4–11 August 2022, which was carried out by China in response to [US Speaker of the House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives "Speaker of the United States House of Representatives") [Nancy Pelosi's visit to Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_visit_by_Nancy_Pelosi_to_Taiwan "2022 visit by Nancy Pelosi to Taiwan"). The drills involved [live-fire drills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_fire_exercise "Live fire exercise"), [air sorties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sortie "Sortie"), naval deployments, and [ballistic missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballistic_missile "Ballistic missile") launches by the [People's Liberation Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army "People's Liberation Army") (PLA), marking China's biggest escalation in the region since the [Third Taiwan Strait Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Taiwan_Strait_Crisis "Third Taiwan Strait Crisis") in 1996.[[4]](#cite_note-China_vows-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-nearby_waters-6)[[7]](#cite_note-2022_biggest_ever-7)

China's military drills were [shows of force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Show_of_force "Show of force") intended to deter what the PRC perceives as US meddling in its internal affairs, and to demonstrate Chinese military power in the region for both international and domestic audiences. The drills drew backlash from the [G7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G7 "G7") (Group of 7) nations.[[6]](#cite_note-nearby_waters-6)[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9) The live-fire drills observed during the seminal August 2022 military exercise were unprecedented in recent history,[[10]](#cite_note-Zheng-10) and took place in seven zones that surrounded the island's busiest [international waterways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_waterways "International waterways") and aviation routes.[[7]](#cite_note-2022_biggest_ever-7)[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-China_adds_7th_zone-12) The first drill came to an end on 11 August 2022.[[13]](#cite_note-drills_over-13)[[14]](#cite_note-completes_tasks-14)

Since then, China has launched at least seven more major military drills targeting Taiwan,[[15]](#cite_note-over_the_years-15)[[16]](#cite_note-through_the_years-16) with PLA exercises, [maritime patrols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_patrol "Maritime patrol") and even [Coast Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Coast_Guard "China Coast Guard") [boardings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_boarding "Naval boarding") around the Taiwan Strait becoming routine in what has been defined as "[grey-zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey-zone_(international_relations) "Grey-zone (international relations)") tactics".[[17]](#cite_note-China_grey-zone_tactics-17) The PRC also declared [sovereignty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereignty "Sovereignty") over all [airspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airspace "Airspace") above and around the island, publicly renouncing the [Davis line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davis_line "Davis line"), an [imaginary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imaginary_line "Imaginary line") median line across the Taiwan Strait that previously marked the *[de facto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_facto "De facto")* [territorial waters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territorial_waters "Territorial waters") between the [mainland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_China "Mainland China") and the island of Taiwan since the 1950s until 2019.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

# Lens 1B.5 — Xi Jinping (China), 2023

**Question:** Did the ruler avoid using nuclear capability to shield conventional aggression, territorial coercion, or domestic repression?

**One-sentence answer for 2023:** The 2023 record is **mostly positive on the formal question** — Xi did **not** publicly threaten nuclear use to shield conventional coercion against Taiwan or the South China Sea, did **not** tie nuclear signaling to the territorial-coercion campaign, and did **not** invoke nuclear capability to justify domestic repression — but with two serious qualifications: (i) the **structural setup** (rapid arsenal growth, launch-on-warning doctrinal drift, PLARF social-media normalization of nuclear strike videos on US and Taiwan targets) implies that the conventional-aggression posture *could* be nuclear-shielded if invoked, and (ii) the **Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis** remained active throughout 2023 under PLA exercises designed to normalize a blockade posture.

---

## A. Claim-level findings — Xi did NOT use nuclear capability to shield coercion in 2023

### 1. No explicit nuclear threat tied to conventional coercion in 2023

- **Claim A1.** Across 2023, Xi Jinping did **not** publicly invoke nuclear weapons, nuclear capability, or nuclear deterrence to shield any conventional coercion — Taiwan, South China Sea, border disputes with India, or maritime disputes with the Philippines. His public statements on Taiwan, the Philippines, and the South China Sea used conventional-arms and political-rhetorical framing (reunification, sovereignty, control measures), not nuclear.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (10 November 2023 entry: "China imposes 'control measures' against Philippine vessels at a contested South China Sea location after a Philippine auxiliary ship entered the area which China deemed as infringing on its sovereignty").
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction (Xi at the 15 November 2023 Biden summit reaffirmed NFU — the rhetorical opposite of nuclear coercion).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.5 (positive — no explicit nuclear-shield rhetoric), 1B.2 (positive — restated).

### 2. No nuclear use to shield South China Sea coercion

- **Claim A2.** China's South China Sea coercion campaign in 2023 — exemplified by the 10 November 2023 "control measures" against Philippine vessels at Second Thomas Shoal and similar grey-zone operations — was conducted **without** any associated nuclear signaling. The instruments were China Coast Guard vessels, PLAN auxiliaries, and maritime sovereignty rhetoric; not PLARF activity, not nuclear-capable bomber flights, not missile tests over contested waters.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China ("10 November – China imposes 'control measures' against Philippine vessels at a contested South China Sea location after a Philippine auxiliary ship entered the area which China deemed as infringing on its sovereignty").
  - **Source:** "South China Sea disputes" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea_disputes (records the conventional character of the disputes through 2023; no nuclear-shielding language recorded).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.5 (positive — no nuclear-shield use), 8G.5.

### 3. No nuclear use to shield Taiwan coercion

- **Claim A3.** Throughout 2023, the **Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis** continued (dating from August 2022), with PLA exercises, ADIZ incursions, and grey-zone operations conducted around Taiwan. None of these exercises or incursions were publicly framed by Xi or by CMC statements as nuclear-shielded. Xi's Taiwan statements remained conventional in language (reunification, anti-independence, one-China principle).
  - **Source:** "Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Taiwan_Strait_Crisis ("China initiated military maneuvers around Taiwan on 2 August 2022, before launching their first major military drill on 4–11 August 2022 … PLA exercises, maritime patrols and even Coast Guard boardings around the Taiwan Strait becoming routine in what has been defined as 'grey-zone tactics'" — the 2023 pattern is a continuation; no nuclear-shielding language).
  - **Source:** "2023 in Taiwan" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_Taiwan (no nuclear event involving PRC–Taiwan in 2023).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.5 (positive — no nuclear-shield use), 8G.6.

### 4. No nuclear use to shield domestic repression in 2023

## B. Claim-level findings — qualifications that complicate the positive reading

### 6. The structural setup creates a latent nuclear shield

- **Claim A6.** Although Xi did not invoke nuclear capability to shield coercion in 2023, the **structural posture of the arsenal** during 2023 created the conditions under which nuclear-shielding would be credible if a crisis required it: the only NPT nuclear-weapon state significantly expanding its arsenal; new ICBM silo fields (Gansu, Xinjiang, plus additional fields); launch-on-warning doctrinal drift; a triad (land/sea/air) becoming fully operational; and the documented 2023 PLARF social-media simulations depicting nuclear strikes on US and Taiwan targets. A ruler who escalates conventional coercion while simultaneously building a launch-on-warning nuclear posture has built the latent shield even if he did not invoke it in 2023.

## C. Net reading for lens 1B.5

The 2023 record is **mostly positive on the surface** but **mixed once structural factors are weighted**:

- **Surface positive:** No explicit nuclear threat attached to Taiwan coercion, South China Sea coercion, or domestic repression; consistent NFU rhetoric; no recorded use of nuclear signaling to shield conventional operations; the PLARF leadership purge created a temporary C2 gap that reduced the credibility of any shield attempt.
- **Structural negative:** Continued arsenal expansion, launch-on-warning doctrinal drift, latent strategic ambiguity about Taiwan, PLARF social-media nuclear-strike simulations (including on Taiwan targets) under PLA accounts without public repudiation, and the overlap of conventional and nuclear operational chains under Xi's CMC chairmanship.

A truly strong ruler on this lens would have used 2023 — with the PLARF in turmoil and US relations at a low point — to **clarify** that nuclear weapons would not be considered in any Taiwan contingency, and to publicly repudiate the PLARF nuclear-strike social-media videos. Xi did neither. He instead maintained structural ambiguity while exercising aggressive conventional coercion.

**Net judgment: 1B.5 reads as positive on the formal question (no explicit nuclear-shield rhetoric or use in 2023) but mixed-to-negative once structural shield-credibility is weighted in. The latent shield was strengthened, even though the explicit shield was not invoked.**
